title: Norway retained a route to cuts without making the next cut urgent
summary: Norges Bank’s January release preserved a conditional easing outlook and an explicitly restrictive current stance. The Committee kept the policy rate at 4% at its 21 January meeting and published the decision on 22 January. Its December forecast had been consistent with one or two cuts during 2026. With no new forecast prepared, the Committee judged that the interest-rate outlook had changed little. Governor Ida Wolden Bache emphasised that the Bank could take time before delivering another cut. A forecast that includes easing somewhere in the year gives little information about the next meeting by itself.

The reason for patience was persistent domestic inflation despite visible cooling in the economy. Inflation excluding energy had stayed close to 3% since autumn 2024, compared with a 2% inflation target over time. Earlier tightening had helped lower overall inflation and slow activity. Capacity utilisation was now close to normal and unemployment had increased somewhat. The rate had already fallen from 4.5% to 4% in 2025. The Committee’s problem was to decide how much additional restraint remained necessary after those cuts, balancing the cost of letting inflation persist against the risk of unnecessary weakness in activity.

The Bank gave specific conditions that could invalidate the December path. Greater weakness in the labour market or faster progress toward the price target could justify faster easing. More persistent growth in business costs or a weaker-than-expected krone could require a higher rate than projected. In that comparison, higher can mean fewer cuts than the baseline. It need not imply moving above the current 4%. The currency matters because higher domestic-currency costs for imported goods can offset disinflation generated by softer local demand.

Geopolitical uncertainty widened the range of possible outcomes but did not itself change the central view. The next meeting, on which new forecasts would be published on 26 March, offered an opportunity to revisit both the path and the indicators conditioning it. The release contains neither market-implied probabilities nor an announcement-day currency move. Those data would be necessary to establish whether investors had expected an earlier cut than the Committee was prepared to suggest.

questions.question: How much easing was priced before the January hold?
questions.detail: Compare meeting-specific krone forward rates with the December path and distinguish expected timing from the expected total number of cuts. A delayed first move can alter short maturities materially even if the expected year-end level changes little.

questions.question: Was the near-3% energy-excluding inflation clustered in domestic components?
questions.detail: Track domestic goods and services prices, business costs and imported goods separately, alongside effective exchange rates. This would help distinguish persistent domestic price setting from a currency-driven offset to disinflation and indicate which risk to the published path was gaining importance.

questions.question: How clearly had activity slowed toward normal capacity?
questions.detail: Compare unemployment, vacancies and business reports of capacity constraints with output and employment. If unemployment was rising faster than implied by other indicators, the case for faster easing would be stronger than the aggregate inflation reading alone suggested.
